paragraphs: Alice was getting very tired of sitting beside her sister on the riverbank with nothing to do. Once or twice she had peeked at the book her sister was reading, but it had no pictures or dialogue in it. “What’s the use of a book,” thought Alice, “without pictures or conversations?”

So she was trying to decide, as best she could (the heat had made her feel sleepy and slow), whether making a daisy chain was worth the effort of getting up to pick the daisies, when suddenly a White Rabbit with pink eyes ran right past her.

There was nothing especially remarkable about that, and Alice didn’t think it was all that strange to hear the Rabbit mutter to itself, “Oh dear! Oh dear! I’m going to be late!” (When she thought it over afterwards, it occurred to her that she should have been surprised, but at the time it all seemed perfectly natural.) But when the Rabbit actually took a watch out of its waistcoat pocket, looked at it, and then hurried on, Alice jumped to her feet. It had just struck her that she had never seen a rabbit with a waistcoat pocket, or with a watch to take out of it. Burning with curiosity, she raced across the field after it, and was just in time to see it dive into a large rabbit hole under the hedge.
A moment later Alice went down after it, never stopping to think how she would ever get out again.

The rabbit hole ran straight ahead like a tunnel for a while, and then dropped away so suddenly that Alice had no time to think about stopping before she found herself falling down what seemed to be a very deep well.

Either the well was extremely deep, or she was falling very slowly, because she had plenty of time to look around and wonder what would happen next. First she tried to look down to see where she was headed, but it was too dark to make anything out. Then she looked at the sides of the well and noticed that they were lined with cupboards and bookshelves, with maps and pictures hanging here and there on pegs. As she passed, she took a jar down from one of the shelves. The label said “ORANGE MARMALADE,” but, to her great disappointment, it was empty. She didn’t want to drop it for fear of hurting someone below, so she managed to tuck it into one of the cupboards as she fell past.

“Well!” thought Alice. “After a fall like this, tumbling down the stairs will be nothing! They’ll think I’m so brave at home! Why, I wouldn’t say a word about it even if I fell off the roof!” (Which was probably true.)

Down, down, down. Would the fall never end? “I wonder how many miles I’ve fallen by now?” she said aloud. “I must be getting close to the center of the earth. Let me see: that would be about four thousand miles down, I think—” (You see, Alice had learned a few things like this in her lessons at school. It wasn’t the best moment to show off her knowledge, since there was no one to hear her, but it was good practice to say it all over.) “—yes, that’s about the right distance—but I wonder what latitude and longitude I’ve reached?” (Alice had no idea what latitude was, or longitude either, but she thought they were nice, impressive words to say.)

Soon she started again. “I wonder if I’ll fall right through the earth! How funny it will be to come out among the people who walk upside down! The Antipathies, I think—” (She was rather glad no one was listening this time, because it didn’t sound like quite the right word.) “—but I’ll have to ask them the name of the country, you know. Excuse me, ma’am, is this New Zealand or Australia?” (And she tried to curtsy as she spoke. Imagine curtsying while you’re falling through the air! Do you think you could manage it?) “And what a silly little girl she’ll think I am for asking! No, I can’t ask. Maybe I’ll see it written up somewhere.”

Down, down, down. There was nothing else to do, so Alice soon started talking again. “Dinah will miss me terribly tonight, I think!” (Dinah was the cat.) “I hope they remember her saucer of milk at teatime. Dinah, my dear, I wish you were down here with me! I’m afraid there are no mice in the air, but you might catch a bat, and that’s very like a mouse, you know. But do cats eat bats, I wonder?” And here Alice began to feel rather sleepy, and went on murmuring to herself in a dreamy way, “Do cats eat bats? Do cats eat bats?” and sometimes, “Do bats eat cats?” Since she couldn’t answer either question, it didn’t much matter which way she asked it. She felt herself dozing off, and had just begun to dream that she was walking hand in hand with Dinah, asking her very earnestly, “Now, Dinah, tell me the truth: did you ever eat a bat?” when suddenly, thump! thump! she landed on a heap of sticks and dry leaves, and the fall was over.

Alice wasn’t hurt at all, and she jumped to her feet at once. She looked up, but it was all dark overhead. In front of her was another long passage, and the White Rabbit was still in sight, hurrying down it. There was not a moment to lose. Away went Alice like the wind, and she was just in time to hear it say, as it turned a corner, “Oh my ears and whiskers, how late it’s getting!” She was right behind it when she turned the corner, but the Rabbit was gone. She found herself in a long, low hall, lit by a row of lamps hanging from the ceiling.

There were doors all around the hall, but every one of them was locked. When Alice had gone all the way down one side and back up the other, trying each door, she walked sadly down the middle, wondering how she would ever get out.

Suddenly she came upon a little three-legged table made entirely of solid glass. There was nothing on it except a tiny golden key, and Alice’s first thought was that it might belong to one of the doors in the hall. But, alas, either the locks were too big or the key was too small, and it wouldn’t open any of them. On her second time around, though, she noticed a low curtain she hadn’t seen before, and behind it was a little door about fifteen inches high. She tried the golden key in the lock, and to her great delight, it fit!

Alice opened the door and found a small passage, not much bigger than a rat hole. She knelt down and looked along it into the loveliest garden you ever saw. How she longed to get out of that dark hall and wander among those beds of bright flowers and cool fountains! But she couldn’t even get her head through the doorway. “And even if my head did fit,” thought poor Alice, “it would be of very little use without my shoulders. Oh, how I wish I could fold up like a telescope! I think I could, if only I knew how to begin.” So many strange things had happened lately that Alice had begun to think very few things were truly impossible.

There seemed no point in waiting by the little door, so she went back to the table, half hoping to find another key on it, or at least a book of rules for folding people up like telescopes. This time she found a little bottle on it (“which certainly wasn’t here before,” said Alice), and tied around its neck was a paper label with the words “DRINK ME” beautifully printed on it in large letters.

It was all very well to say “Drink me,” but sensible little Alice wasn’t going to do that in a hurry. “No, I’ll look first,” she said, “and see whether it’s marked ‘poison’ or not.” She had read several nice little stories about children who had been burned, or eaten by wild animals, or met other unpleasant ends, all because they wouldn’t remember the simple rules their friends had taught them: for example, that a red-hot poker will burn you if you hold it too long, and that if you cut your finger very deeply with a knife, it usually bleeds. And she had never forgotten that if you drink a lot from a bottle marked “poison,” it is almost certain to disagree with you sooner or later.

However, this bottle was not marked “poison,” so Alice risked a taste. Finding it very nice (it had a sort of mixed flavor of cherry tart, custard, pineapple, roast turkey, toffee, and hot buttered toast), she very soon finished it off.
“What a curious feeling!” said Alice. “I must be folding up like a telescope.”

And so she was: she was now only ten inches tall, and her face lit up at the thought that she was now the right size to go through the little door into that lovely garden. First, though, she waited a few minutes to see if she would shrink any further. She felt a bit nervous about this. “Because it might end, you know,” Alice said to herself, “with me disappearing altogether, like a candle. I wonder what I’d be like then?” And she tried to imagine what the flame of a candle looks like after the candle is blown out, since she couldn’t remember ever having seen such a thing.

After a while, when nothing more happened, she decided to go into the garden right away. But, poor Alice! When she reached the door, she found she had forgotten the little golden key, and when she went back to the table for it, she found she couldn’t possibly reach it. She could see it quite clearly through the glass, and she tried her best to climb up one of the table legs, but it was too slippery. When she had worn herself out with trying, the poor little thing sat down and cried.

“Come on, there’s no use crying like that!” Alice said to herself, rather sharply. “I advise you to stop this minute!” She usually gave herself very good advice (though she very seldom followed it), and sometimes she scolded herself so harshly that she brought tears to her eyes. Once she even remembered trying to box her own ears for cheating in a game of croquet she was playing against herself, because this curious child was very fond of pretending to be two people. “But it’s no use pretending to be two people now,” thought poor Alice. “Why, there’s hardly enough of me left to make one respectable person!”

Soon her eye fell on a little glass box lying under the table. She opened it and found a very small cake inside, with the words “EAT ME” beautifully marked on it in currants. “Well, I’ll eat it,” said Alice, “and if it makes me grow bigger, I can reach the key, and if it makes me grow smaller, I can creep under the door. Either way I’ll get into the garden, and I don’t care which happens!”

She ate a little bit and said anxiously to herself, “Which way? Which way?” She held her hand on top of her head to feel which way she was growing, and she was quite surprised to find that she stayed the same size. That is what usually happens when you eat cake, of course, but Alice had gotten so used to expecting nothing but strange things that it seemed dull and stupid for life to go on in the ordinary way.
So she set to work and very soon finished off the cake.
